topic: The fall of Blockbuster and the Netflix deal it rejected
title: Blockbuster Could Have Bought Netflix for $50 Million
alt_titles: How Blockbuster Went From 9,000 Stores to Just One
The $50 Million Mistake That Killed Blockbuster
pinned_comment: If you were Blockbuster's CEO in 2000, would you have paid 50 million dollars for Netflix? Be honest.
sources_to_check: Netflix's 2000 offer to Blockbuster for about 50 million dollars (reported by Marc Randolph and others)
Blockbuster peak of about 9,000 stores in 2004
Late fees of about 800 million dollars in 2000
Bankruptcy in September 2010 and sale to Dish Network in 2011 for about 320 million dollars
description:
In the year 2000, Netflix offered itself to Blockbuster for 50 million dollars. Blockbuster said no. This is the full story of how the king of home entertainment went from 9,000 stores to a single shop in Oregon.

Blockbuster had everything: the brand, the customers, the money and even a working online service that was beating Netflix. So how did it lose? In this video we go through the late fees that made it rich and hated at the same time, the meeting in Dallas that changed business history, the boardroom war that killed its best idea, and the lesson every company can learn from it.

• How Blockbuster became a 9,000-store empire
• The late fees that paid for everything
• The Netflix meeting in Dallas
• Total Access: the plan that almost worked
• Bankruptcy and the last store on Earth

segments.text: In the year 2000, three men flew to Dallas to sell their tiny company. They asked for 50 million dollars. The CEO on the other side of the table listened politely, and then, according to the people in that room, he tried very hard not to laugh. The tiny company was Netflix. The company that said no was Blockbuster. Today Netflix is worth hundreds of billions of dollars, and Blockbuster has exactly one store left on the entire planet.

How does a company with thousands of stores, millions of customers and billions in revenue lose to a startup that mailed DVDs in red envelopes? The answer is not what most people think. Because Blockbuster did not ignore the internet. In fact, at one point, Blockbuster was actually winning. And that is the part of the story almost nobody tells.

Let's go back to 1985. In Dallas, Texas, a businessman called David Cook opens a video rental store with a simple idea. Most rental shops back then were small, messy and dark, with a few hundred tapes. Cook wanted something different: huge, bright stores with thousands of titles, and a computer system to track every single tape. People loved it. Two years later, a businessman named Wayne Huizenga bought control of the company, and he did not want a successful chain. He wanted an empire.

And he built one. Under Huizenga, Blockbuster opened stores at an incredible pace, at one point roughly one new store every day. By the mid nineties it was a global brand, and in 1994 the media giant Viacom bought it for around eight billion dollars. Friday night in America had a ritual: you drove to Blockbuster, walked the aisles, argued with your family about what to watch, and grabbed popcorn at the checkout.

But behind that ritual there was a secret. Blockbuster was not only making money when you rented a movie. It was making a fortune when you returned it late. In the year 2000, late fees brought in around 800 million dollars, more than a tenth of the company's revenue. Think about that. A huge part of the business depended on its own customers messing up, and customers hated it.

Blockbuster also had enormous power over Hollywood. In the late nineties, customers were furious because new releases were always out of stock. So in 1998 Blockbuster signed revenue sharing deals with the big studios. Instead of paying a high price for each tape, it paid less up front and shared the rental money with the studios. Suddenly stores could have dozens of copies of every new hit, and the slogan became simple: guaranteed to be there. Profits went up again. On paper, nothing could stop this company.

One of those angry customers was a software entrepreneur called Reed Hastings. As the story goes, he once kept a copy of Apollo 13 too long and got hit with a 40 dollar late fee. His co-founder Marc Randolph later said the story was simplified, but the idea behind it was real: what if renting movies had no late fees at all? In 1997 they started Netflix. You chose DVDs on a website, they arrived by mail, and you kept them as long as you wanted.

Now, this sounds brilliant today, but back then Netflix was losing money fast. By 2000 the dot com bubble was bursting and investors were running away. So Hastings and Randolph had an idea: sell Netflix to the biggest name in the business. They flew to Dallas to meet Blockbuster's CEO, John Antioco. Their pitch was simple. Netflix would run Blockbuster's online brand, Blockbuster would promote Netflix in its stores, and the price was 50 million dollars.

Antioco was not impressed. Remember, Blockbuster was making billions. The internet was full of companies burning cash, and Netflix looked like one more. Why pay 50 million dollars for a website that mailed discs and lost money? The meeting ended, and the founders flew home with nothing. But that was not the worst decision Blockbuster would make. The worst one came later, when it had already fixed its mistake.

Because here is the twist. Blockbuster did not stay asleep. Over the next few years, it watched Netflix grow and it finally reacted. In 2004 it launched its own online DVD service. It also did something painful: it eliminated late fees, walking away from hundreds of millions of dollars. And in 2006, it launched something called Total Access. You could rent online, and return the DVD in any store for a free movie on the spot. Netflix could not do that. It had no stores.

And it worked. Total Access grew quickly, reaching millions of subscribers. Netflix executives have admitted they were worried. Some of them believed that if Blockbuster kept going, it could win. If you are enjoying this story, subscribe, because we break down one of these corporate disasters every week. Now, back to Dallas. Blockbuster finally had a winning strategy. So what happened?

What happened was money and ego. Eliminating late fees and funding Total Access was expensive, and the profits went down. The billionaire investor Carl Icahn, who owned a large stake, clashed with Antioco over the cost and over the CEO's pay. In 2007, Antioco left the company. The man who replaced him, Jim Keyes, believed the future was still in physical stores. He cut back the online push and focused on retail again.

It was the worst possible moment. Streaming was arriving. In 2007, Netflix started letting people watch movies instantly on their computers. Then the 2008 financial crisis hit, and Blockbuster had a mountain of debt. Store traffic kept falling, month after month. Each empty store still had to pay rent, staff and electricity, while Netflix only needed servers and envelopes.

In September 2010, Blockbuster filed for bankruptcy. The company that once had around 9,000 stores and tens of thousands of employees was sold in 2011 to Dish Network for about 320 million dollars. Store after store closed its doors. By 2014 the last company-owned locations were gone. Only a handful of franchise stores survived, and one by one they also disappeared.

Except one. In Bend, Oregon, a single Blockbuster is still open. It is run by a local manager, it rents real movies, and it has become a tourist attraction. People travel from all over the world just to take a photo in front of the blue and yellow sign. It is the last store on Earth of a company that could have owned Netflix for less than what some footballers earn in a year.

And here is an irony most people forget. In 2011, Netflix almost made its own Blockbuster mistake. It raised prices and tried to split its DVD business into a separate service called Qwikster. Customers were furious, and Netflix lost around 800,000 subscribers in just a few months. Its stock crashed. But unlike Blockbuster, Reed Hastings publicly apologized, cancelled the plan within weeks, and went all in on streaming. Netflix was willing to hurt its old business to protect its future. Blockbuster never was.

So what is the real lesson here? Blockbuster's problem was not that it did not see the future. It saw it, it built it, and it was even winning. The problem was that the future was less profitable than the present, and the people in charge were not willing to sacrifice today's money for tomorrow's business. Netflix had nothing to lose. Blockbuster had everything to lose, and that is exactly why it lost.

Today, you probably open Netflix without thinking about it. But somewhere in Oregon, there is a blue and yellow sign reminding us that no company is too big to fall. Now I want to know what you think. If you had been in that room in Dallas in the year 2000, would you have bought Netflix for 50 million dollars? Tell me in the comments.

segments.text: In 2000, Netflix asked Blockbuster for 50 million dollars. Blockbuster basically laughed them out of the room. At the time, Blockbuster had thousands of stores and made around 800 million dollars a year just from late fees. Netflix was a small website losing money. Ten years later, Blockbuster was bankrupt. Today Netflix is worth hundreds of billions, and Blockbuster has one single store left, in Oregon. But here is the crazy part: Blockbuster almost won anyway. The full story is on the channel.
